name: Sherlock's bet to Moriarty
description: Sherlock met Moriarty for a final battle of wits. He gave him a regular n sided convex polygon. In addition to it, he gave him certain diagonals to form regions on the polygon. It was guaranteed that the diagonals did not intersect in interior points. He took each of the region and calculated its importance value. Importance value for a region formed by vertices a 1 , a 2 , ... , a x of the polygon will be given by 2 a 1 + 2 a 2 + ... + 2 a x . Then, he sorted these regions on the basis of their importance value in ascending order. After that he assigned each region an index from 1 to k , where k is the number of regions, and index of region is its position in the sorted array calculated above. He wants Moriarty to color the regions using not more than 20 colors, such that two regions have same color only if all the simple paths between these two regions have at least one region with color value less than the color value assigned to these regions. Simple path between two regions f and h is a sequence of regions r 1 , r 2 , ... r t such that r 1 = f , r t = h , for each 1 ≤ i < t regions r i and r i + 1 share an edge, and r i = r j if and only if i = j . Moriarty couldn't answer and asks Sherlock to solve it himself. Help Sherlock in doing so.
input_specification: First line contains two integers n and m ( 3 ≤ n ≤ 100000 , 0 ≤ m ≤ n - 3 ), the number of vertices in the polygon and the number of diagonals added. Each of the next m lines contains two integers a and b ( 1 ≤ a , b ≤ n ), describing a diagonal between vertices a and b . It is guaranteed that the diagonals are correct, i. e. a and b don't coincide and are not neighboring. It is guaranteed that the diagonals do not intersect.
output_specification: Let the number of regions be k . Output k space-separated integers, each between 1 and 20 , representing the colors of the regions in the order of increasing importance. If there are multiple answers, print any of them. It can be shown that at least one answer exists.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 776F — Sherlock's bet to Moriarty [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
